articles.title: 29 New Changes in the Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake — Redesigned Puzzles, Updated Miniboss Fights, and Deeper Dialogue
articles.summary: I played more than an hour of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, and as someone who’s finished the original several times, I noticed a lot of small changes that shine some light on the thought process behind recreating this adventure. It seems everything was on the table when considering what to tweak: altered puzzles more closely fit the modern controls, redesigned miniboss fights spice things up across each round, and new shortcuts and context clues make navigation more intuitive.
articles.body:
I played more than an hour of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2, and as someone who’s finished the original several times, I noticed a lot of small changes that shine some light on the thought process behind recreating this adventure. It seems everything was on the table when considering what to tweak: altered puzzles more closely fit the modern controls, redesigned miniboss fights spice things up across each round, and new shortcuts and context clues make navigation more intuitive. If you’re dying to learn every detail you can about Ocarina of Time before its November 5 release date , I’m going to list a bunch of notable differences I saw when comparing it to the N64 original. Before we start, a couple of notes:

First, this article is not my official preview – you can check out my more formal first impression of Ocarina of Time here , and watch this week’s Nintendo Voice Chat where I dive even further into it.

Second, this is far from an exhaustive list of differences. I’m mostly leaving out the really obvious things like controls, art style, and voice acting (you can read up on things like that in the prequel to this piece ), and this would take far too long to write if I catalogued every difference there is. I’m only bringing up a change I already pointed out if I was able to officially confirm it through gameplay or learned something new worth sharing.

Third, we’re restricted on how many screenshots we’re allowed to publish for this preview period, so for this piece, you’ll have to rely on the written word alone. We’re going old school!

Finally, and most importantly, there will be spoilers for the original Ocarina of Time as we dive into the changes I saw in Kokiri Forest, Inside the Great Deku Tree, Hyrule Field, Castle Town, and the Forest Temple. It’s kind of hard to discuss changes without explaining the source material! If you don’t know the original, don’t want to be reminded of it, or don’t want to see how some things play out differently, this is not for you! Okay, that’s more than enough preamble – let’s get started.

1. Link’s wallet can hold 200 rupees from the very beginning, as opposed to the N64’s starting limit of 99.

2. Jumping across the stone platforms next to the Kokiri Forest shop no longer rewards you with a secret five rupees. Instead, additional blue rupees are scattered throughout the forest.

3. Speaking of the shop, there’s a new scarecrow training dummy to the right of the counter. A villager uses it to run you through a quick tutorial on raising your defenses.

4. The challenge to obtain the Kokiri Sword has been overhauled. The treasure chest used to be tucked in the back corner of the room; now it’s placed high on a platform in the middle. You have to jump to it instead of practicing reorienting the camera to reach it. I dive into more of the philosophy behind this change in my preview .

Inside the Great Deku Tree (Child Link Dungeon)

5. In the room where you get the slingshot, a second, smaller treasure chest used to hold a random recovery heart. It was always kind of a disappointing reveal, in my opinion. Now, it holds a few Deku Nuts. I think that’s a slight improvement!

6. You fight a lot of Skulltulas in the Great Deku Tree, and their attack patterns have changed. Rather than just deciding to occasionally reveal their weak spot to you, whacking them with your sword sends them spinning around, exposing their soft underbelly. This fits in line with Ocarina of Time’s newfound focus on logic: an enemy doesn’t give you an unearned opening anymore -- you have to trigger it.

7. On N64, Lon Lon Ranch kind of looked like an impenetrable fortress from the outside, with high walls you couldn’t really see over. Now, it’s more naturally woven into the environment, and you can spy the horses grazing from outside.

8. Peahat enemies decorated the corners of Hyrule Field in the original, but on my way to Castle Town, I ran into a few that were more centrally located. A Hyrule Field populated with more enemies is a good thing in my book.

9. Near the new Peahats, I saw a cracked piece of the ground that looked perfect for a bomb. Most entrances to hidden rooms in the original were completely invisible to the naked eye – this is a much clearer hint towards a secret area. I can’t wait to see what those sparse caves look like now.

10. In my last “Biggest Changes” piece for Ocarina of Time, I noticed a new sign right outside of the Castle Town gate. I was wondering if it would provide new lore surrounding the history of Hyrule, the events of Skyward Sword, or something like that. But, it’s just a large sign pointing you in the direction of Hyrule Field’s biggest landmarks. Not really what I was hoping for, but a noteworthy change nonetheless.

11. The biggest difference in Castle Town is its perspective shift. It’s no longer restricted to fixed camera angles; it’s in third-person with complete camera control the whole time. You can even seamlessly walk all the way from the town’s entrance to the Temple of Time with no loading screens or camera breaks.

12. Upon entering Castle Town, I spoke to a new NPC: a blonde woman who warns Link not to spend all his money, even though there are so many exciting options at the market. This is just the first visit to the town, so I’m hopeful she’ll have some sort of additional quest or dialogue later on.

Last spoiler warning here – some of the puzzle changes in the Forest Temple are fairly significant!

13. There are a ton of minor changes to how the Forest Temple looks and functions, and it starts right at the entrance. Instead of hookshotting onto a tree branch, Link aims at a more traditional hookshot target above the temple’s front door. Pairing this with a similar example, where in the Great Deku Tree Link shoots an eyeball target instead of a ladder, it seems the remake is more intent on teaching us how to use these items on recognizable, intended targets rather than parts of the world players might not think to interact with.

14. After completing a puzzle that involves pushing blocks and climbing ladders to get to the top of a room, you can now activate a brand new elevator that makes it so you don’t have to walk through all the same tunnels and climb the same ladders on repeat visits.

15. Floormasters – the iconic disembodied hand enemies that stalk Link from the ceiling – are now telegraphed by a bright spotlight that shines on Link and changes color just before the hand swoops down. It’s very cool, and fits this remake’s theatrical vibe I dive into in my preview .

16. This one is also from my preview: “An arena where Link fights a Stalfos used to have a giant hole in the middle. Link needed to avoid it or risk falling to the floor below, but the Stalfos could defy gravity and hover over the gap… Here, that hole has been exchanged for a shallow pool of acid. The skeleton enemies can still walk in it – they don’t have any flesh to lose – while Link takes damage if he enters it. This means the fight plays out the same as it used to: the Stalfos has access to the whole room while Link is constrained to its edges, but the way it’s constructed is more logical.”

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Preview Screenshots

17. The rooms and hallways on the side of the mansion with the red Poe have red carpeting and stained glass windows, while their counterparts on the side with the blue Poe have blue carpeting and windows. This really differentiates how otherwise similar rooms look and feel, and makes it so you are probably less likely to get lost.

18. A torch puzzle that used to involve spinning platforms has been redone without the rotating elements.

19. In the room where a giant block crashes onto the floor, guard rails have been added to prevent Link from leaping onto the block before it rises back to the ceiling. You couldn’t jump at the press of a button on N64! I imagine the developers had to rethink a lot of the world’s geometry now that Link can jump at any time.

20. The encounters with the final two Poes have been remixed. The sliding block puzzle to reveal the green Poe no longer has a time limit, but the extra block that’s meant to fake you out is slightly more interesting now. The moments leading up to the fight with the final Poe, and the fight itself, have been fleshed out. There’s an entirely new cutscene, and each round of the fight is unique, rather than having the exact same pattern repeat itself three times.

21. The final room before facing the Forest Temple’s boss used to be about rotating the inner wall of a cylinder to gain access to specific rooms on the outer wall. That concept is still intact, but it now involves torches as well.

22. I really noticed the expanded dialogue from characters throughout my preview session. Everyone had more to say: Link’s friends seemed to know him a bit better, the Kokiri shopkeeper had beef with Mido, Castle Town villagers seemed more enthralled with this mysterious forest boy, and a few cutscenes I saw had voice acting. There are also more dialogue choices than before that are reminiscent of Link’s snarkier tone in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

23. When casting the Din’s Fire attack spell, the whole world would come to a stop on N64. Now, the spell is cast in real time, meaning you need to make sure you’re not at risk of getting hit before using it.

24. Like the 3DS remaster, you can quickly open a songbook when playing the Ocarina to remind yourself of the button prompts for each specific song, rather than having to go all the way into the pause menu.

25. The original Ocarina of Time had four empty bottles to collect. On the remake’s inventory menu, there are clearly five slots for empty bottles. I confirmed this extra slot when playing, meaning there’s an additional bottle involved somehow in Link’s quest.

26. Speaking of the inventory screen, here’s a fun fact: the top left quadrant is reserved for items only Child Link can equip, while the top right quadrant is for Adult Link’s tools. The bottom half has items both of them can use, and there are dividing lines clearly separating these three areas.

27. When the hookshot lines up with an enemy it can strike, the target reticle color changes from blue to red, giving you an easy way to see that your shot will land.

28. A quest log lightly guides you where to go next (if you need it – I wasn’t required to open it a single time), and adds flavor text to the adventure. Quest descriptions are written like old legends – “There once was a boy named Link…” – which I find very fitting.

29. Lastly, I have to shout out the music, which was just a joy to listen to during my preview. From the bright Kokiri Forest theme to the adventurous Hyrule Field tune, hearing these classic songs brought to life by recordings of real musicians was a treat. I can’t wait to hear the rest of the soundtrack.

And that’s it! If you can believe it, we’re just over three weeks away from playing the Ocarina of Time remake for ourselves. Before you go, remember to check out my official hands-on preview and this week’s episode of Nintendo Voice Chat . Also, this piece is exactly 1998 words, which is the year Ocarina of Time originally released on Nintendo 64. There’s one more fun fact for you!

Logan Plant is IGN's Senior Editor, Playlist and DB, and the host of Nintendo Voice Chat. The Legend of Zelda is his favorite video game franchise of all time, and he is patiently awaiting the day Nintendo announces a brand new F-Zero. You can find new episodes of NVC on the IGN Games YouTube channel, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app.

articles.title: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is almost the Android tablet we needed
articles.summary: Amazon’s latest tablet has a lovely screen, is well made, and runs full Android. But it’s too full of Amazon to really recommend.
articles.body: We have to talk about this screen. It’s the first thing you notice, and maybe the only thing that matters, about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. It’s a 12-inch, 2800 x 1840 panel with a new technology Amazon calls “Nanomatte” that is meant to decrease glare and increase the feeling that you can reach out and touch the things you see onscreen. When Amazon set out to build the best tablet the company has ever shipped, it started with this screen. The $549.99 device I’ve been testing is one of four new models in the Alexa Tablet lineup, which ranges from a $229.99 8-inch model up to a $679.99 12 Pro with this Nanomatte coating and some extra RAM you don’t really need. The pitch for all those devices is the same: They’re well-made, midrange tablets that can access the full universe of Android apps through the Play Store and come with a whole bunch of Amazon bloatware whether you want it or not. I haven’t tested those other devices, but I’m glad they exist — cheap, good Android tablets are too hard to come by. [Product: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro | But the Nanomatte. The Nanomatte! The etching on the display, which Amazon says it partnered with Corning to do at a sub-pixel level to reduce glare without causing the slight rainbow-shimmering effect you can get on other matte screens, absolutely does its job. When I use my iPad outdoors, I can often see what’s behind me like I’m staring into a mirror; the 12 Pro reflects only a small sheen of light, and does it without losing any sharpness. The viewing angles are incredible, too. I’d like the display to be a little brighter, but since the main reason to crank the brightness is to fight glare, it hasn’t really been a problem. The screen is not perfect. The anti-glare texture gives the Alexa Tablet a bit of shimmer, especially when you’re looking at light text on a black background. And the iPad’s blacks are still blacker; watching a movie, the letterboxes above and below are still slightly lit on the Alexa Tablet’s LCD, and they’re just flat-out off on the iPad’s OLED panel. Some of this you can fix: The 12 Pro has specific modes that automatically tweak tone and color to make reading more pleasant, and you can even control the overall picture through a few presets like the ones you’d find on your TV. My review unit came with “Boosted” mode turned on, which made every color just a smidge too colorful. I turned it to “Natural” and immediately liked the picture better. [Image: This is as nice a reading tablet as you’ll find anywhere. I’m not sure this screen counts as some revolution in display technology, but then again, I did reflexively say “whoa” the first second I turned it on, and all that was showing was the Amazon logo. I like this display for everything. The 120Hz refresh rate looks great when running Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and the 3:2 aspect ratio feels right for web browsing and side-by-side work. The more muted display modes even make reading more pleasant than your average giant screen, though it’s lame that they only work in the Kindle app. After a few days of using the tablet indoors and out, I prefer the 12 Pro’s screen to any iPad I’ve tried. (Unfortunately, I don’t have an iPad Pro with the nano-texture glass to compare it to, but that’s a $2,200 tablet. I doubt anyone’s debating between the two.) All that display tech in a $549.99 device requires tradeoffs basically everywhere else, and Amazon makes lots of them. The MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor benchmarks somewhere between a flagship high-end Android phone from last year and a flagship phone from two years ago, and gets absolutely lapped by practically every current iPad. In one graphics-heavy benchmark, the current 13-inch iPad Pro scored about nine times higher. I’d like more horsepower here, but in my day-to-day use there’s plenty of power in this tablet. In several days of playing games, doing work, and watching a lot of NFL RedZone, the only slowness I’ve detected has been little niggling things in the Android experience. The app switcher sometimes stutters when it loads. I suppose I worry a little about how this tablet will age, given that it doesn’t share the iPad’s preposterous oversupply of processing power, but for now it’s fine. Come to think of it, “it’s fine” explains most of the 12 Pro’s hardware. The four speakers are a little thin and muddy, but loud and clear enough. The cameras wash out some colors, but they work for video calls. The $149.99 keyboard case is nice to type on, but a little awkward to detach and manipulate. The $89.99 pen is smooth and responsive, but not many Android apps support a stylus. The battery lasts me about eight hours of screen time, which is a little less than I’d like and less than Amazon advertises. Nothing here is a deal-breaker, it’s just a lot of fine. [Image: The Play Store immediately makes this an improvement on Fire tablets. The software, on the other hand, is all extremes. The great news: The Alexa Tablets run full Android, not the weird off-brand operating system Amazon’s Fire tablets have used for the last 15 years. That means you get all the apps in the Play Store, a vastly improved interface, and access to things like Google’s Gemini assistant. All by itself, that change makes these the most functional Amazon tablets ever. Unfortunately, Amazon did to Android exactly what you’d fear — and maybe expect. It Amazon-ed the crap out of things. I’m fine with the slide-over panel to the left of the homescreen filled with content recommendations; the overlap of Alexa Tablet owners and Prime subscribers / Kindle readers is probably pretty high, and at least that screen isn’t staring you in the face every time you unlock your tablet. I can even live with Amazon preloading its own browser, photos, and music apps, none of which are better than their competition. But it is frankly outrageous that Amazon thinks it can get away with adding two separate, non-removable homescreen widgets that serve no purpose other than advertising Amazon’s products. If you’re going to say you “obsess over customers,” you don’t get to borrow the top left corner of my homescreen and then use that space to show me an ad vaguely offering to “Cook with premium ingredients” that launches an also unhideable Alexa chat window in the bottom right corner of my homescreen. Luckily, this is Android, and installing a new launcher takes 30 seconds. If you buy an Alexa Tablet, I recommend doing so immediately. [Image: I do not need Alexa this front and center on my tablet. I would be less annoyed by Alexa’s overbearing presence on this tablet if Alexa Plus were actually useful, which it mostly is not. If you’re looking to buy whatever’s on your screen, Alexa’s your bot: You can invoke the assistant in any app, and it’ll almost always assume your goal is to shop for whatever you’re currently looking at. If you want, well, anything else, you’re probably out of luck. Almost a year after its launch, Alexa Plus is not a very good assistant. It’s slow, it gets lost in back-and-forth conversations, and it still doesn’t have enough access to my apps and data to be useful. You can switch to Gemini in the device’s settings, and you should. Once you de-Amazon the tablet, you’re left with a pretty useful Android device. And this is where the Alexa Tablet gets tricky to evaluate. I wouldn’t recommend using it as a primary computer, given the still sorry state of large-screen Android apps. (Between this and the ongoing Googlebook fiasco, I really hope Google is learning a lesson about incentivizing developers to care about big screens and keyboards.) But between the Kindle-specific display mode, all the streaming and reading apps in the Play Store, and this terrific screen, this is immediately one of the best tablets-for-tablet-things you can buy. Realistically, you’re probably debating whether to buy the Alexa Tablet or an iPad. (Apologies to the Samsung Galaxy Tab shoppers out there, but this one’s a way better buy for almost everybody.) For the same $550 you’ll drop on the 12 Pro, you can get a base-model iPad with 256GB of storage. I’d probably tell you to buy the iPad; it has much better tablet software and much better big-screen apps, and Apple has a much better track record in tablets. And yet for the last few days, I’ve had an iPad and an Alexa Tablet sitting on my desk, and every time I want to watch or read something I’ve found myself gravitating to Amazon’s device. It is really nice to look at.

articles.title: The Ocarina of Time remake feels remarkably modern — and surprisingly terrifying
articles.summary: New tech and gameplay improvements make it easier to get into Nintendo’s defining title.
articles.body: With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time: its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much — 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness — has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it’s shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original. More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Time with modern trappings to make it more welcoming to those who were introduced to Zelda through more modern releases, like Breath of the Wild. The remake has a new progression marker, called Threads of Time, that’s viewable when you pause. It also has Zelda Notes integration within the Nintendo Switch app to let you view game maps and other info on your phone. Oh, it also has a dedicated jump button. I spent around 90 minutes during a recent preview event in New York City playing through some chunks of the game, including when you first take control of Child Link, and later on after you yank the Master Sword in the Temple of Time to become Adult Link. Its story still makes it a standout Zelda title, and the improvements make it even easier to get immersed in. [Image: In some ways, the remake feels similar to modern Zelda games. Link is snappy to control, and lock-on combat is engaging. Swapping between items and weapons no longer requires hopping into the pause menu, as it did in the original. Holding a shoulder button halts the action, and you can navigate with an analog stick to find what you want in near-realtime. However, it’s an adventure on a much smaller scale; the complexity of your quests, and the tools at your disposal for combat and getting around are simpler, but no less fun. All of the sections I played were truncated, though I left feeling confident that Nintendo nailed this remake. My favorite section was the Forest Temple, which really shows off the more realistic art style. It can finally portray the game’s horror themes in ways that weren’t possible 28 years ago. For example, Link traverses rooms in the dungeon that have red stained glass windows, and as he passes through beams of light, he is cast in the color of blood. It really looks and feels like he’s on an adventure to stave off cataclysm, and the visual evolution frequently made me stop playing for a second while I took in the changes. Also, being able to use the right stick to control the camera lets you create cinematic moments on-the-fly, which is great if, like me, you like taking a lot of screenshots. [Image: [Image: Ocarina of Time is one of Nintendo’s most influential games, and playing it is a rite of passage for any Zelda fan, but it can be tough to go back to the original. As accessible as it is considering it was one of Nintendo’s earliest fully-3D titles, the remake makes it so much easier to get into. And it’s launching at a time when the Zelda franchise is bigger than ever. Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom were big sellers, and they continue to attract new players years after launch, while fans will be able to dig into the live-action movie in April 2027. Even sooner, though, Switch 2 owners will get to feast on the best way to play through a defining Zelda classic. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches for the Nintendo Switch 2 on Thursday, November 5th.

articles.title: We might not have to wait 13 years for the next GTA
articles.summary: Rockstar Games said the developer now has the engine, tools, and team in place to work “more quickly” on future projects, Bloomberg reports.
articles.body: Rockstar Games might not keep fans waiting as long for the next installment of Grand Theft Auto. As part of Bloomberg’s expansive report on the making of GTA VI, Rockstar technical lead Phil Hooker said that the “engine, the tools and the team we’ve built during this project will allow us to do things more quickly.” GTA VI had a notoriously long development process. It took eight years to make, leaving a 13-year gap between this upcoming installment and GTA V. The report points to the one-year gap between Grand Theft Auto III and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was possible because Rockstar already had the framework in place for its next project. “I feel confident that we can build on top of this [GTA VI] and go more sideways than upwards to build more compelling content,” Hooker told Bloomberg. There were several other interesting details in the report as well, including: * Rockstar built a studio dedicated to creating nonplayable characters (NPCs) after the team realized it lacked the “production capabilities” needed to write and animate all of the game’s NPCs. That contributed to the game’s delay. “I think when it became apparent that some areas weren’t going to make it, that’s when we decided to make the shift of date,” Hooker said. “We could hit that schedule, but it won’t be the game we want to make.” * GTA VI apparently didn’t cost more than $1.5 billion to develop, as Rockstar’s publishing head Jennifer Kolbe shut down a report that suggested it was more expensive to build than Dubai’s Burj Khalifa. * Rockstar head of development Aaron Garbut responded to the massive GTA VI leak in 2022: “It feels like somebody’s wading through your dirty washing,” Garbut told Bloomberg. “It’s like they’re inside your head. You see your early work out there. Nobody’s ever supposed to see that. It’s really weirdly invasive. And so it’s quite hard to deal with on an emotional level.” * Since 2018, the number of Rockstar employees has risen from 2,441 to 4,711 across 12 offices. GTA VI launches on November 19th on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X | S.

articles.title: Epic is bringing Fortnite to Linux
articles.summary: Epic is working on bringing Fortnite to Linux through its Epic Games Launcher and is rebuilding its Easy Anti-Cheat software.
articles.body: Epic is working on bringing Fortnite to Linux through its Epic Games Launcher. The new launcher is releasing in preview today, and for the first time on Linux, and while Fortnite isn’t available there just yet, Epic wants to make that a reality. So far, part of the reason Fortnite hasn’t been available on Linux is concerns about cheating. While Epic’s Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) service does support Linux, Fortnite itself does not, and in February 2022, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney said that for Fortnite, “We don’t have confidence that we’d be able to combat cheating at scale under a wide array of kernel configurations.” But now, Epic says it’s planning to rebuild EAC for Linux, which it is calling EAC Linux v2. “To bring Fortnite to Linux, we are rebuilding Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) and working with distro maintainers on security requirements,” Epic says in a blog post. “Once it’s working with a critical mass of distro maintainers, we’ll bring Fortnite to Linux via the Epic Games Launcher. We’ll also make these improvements available to other developers so they can bring their games to Linux players.” Epic plans to pilot EAC Linux v2 in Fortnite first, Epic says in a separate post focused on the anti-cheat update. The company doesn’t have a timeline for when the Fortnite Linux version might be available, Epic engineering director Rick Deist tells The Verge in a briefing. Epic is also “investigating” making the game compatible with Valve’s Linux-based SteamOS, Deist says, though the company does not plan to bring Fortnite to Valve’s Steam store, according to Epic Games Store VP and GM Martin Keely. The company also says that the Steam Deck “does not support the required features for our EAC v2 solution, but we are actively talking with Valve and hope to support it in the future.”

articles.title: 'The Library Loads 30x Faster’ – The New, Much Speedier Epic Games Launcher Has Arrived
articles.summary: The newly rebuilt Epic Games Launcher is now available to download in preview, and it promises speedier load times than both the old version and Steam.
articles.body:
Epic has released a new version of the Epic Games Launcher, with a preview version of the company’s refreshed Steam competitor available to download now.

This new Epic Games Launcher, which was built using AI and “vibe coding” , is currently in the early stages of development and so is “light on features” according to a new blog post from Epic . The preview version features the core components you’d expect from a launcher, including store, library, and social panels, as well as the Unreal-focused developer page.

“It's been rebuilt entirely from the ground up,” explained Martin Keely, vice president and general manager of Epic Games Store, in an interview with IGN. “So this is a completely new tech stack, a complete new rewrite of both the shell, which has the download manager, library, and the app itself, as well as the new store architecture. So features like discover and product detail pages, those have all been rewritten.”

In terms of improvements, for this first phase of the rebuild the big focus has been on speed. Epic says that the launcher boots from cold in 5.47 seconds, which it claims is 46% faster than Steam. When re-opening the app from the system tray, it takes just .36 seconds – 14% faster than Steam. These times will surely vary depending on your system specs, but in ideal conditions it does appear the new app is much speedier than its sluggish predecessor.

“The library loads 30 times faster [than in the previous launcher],” said Keely. “The startup is twice as fast. And it's a small footprint, only 300mb. That was another thing that we wanted to continue to make as small as possible to support the wide range of hardware that players have.”

For this new version of the launcher, Epic is supporting Windows, MacOS, and, for the first time, Linux. That also means that Fortnite is coming to Linux, although it’s not available quite yet – Epic first needs to rebuild its Easy Anti-Cheat system for the platform . “Once it’s working with a critical mass of distro maintainers, we’ll bring Fortnite to Linux via the Epic Games Launcher,” explained Epic’s blog post.

Beyond the speed and platform upgrades, the new launcher features some much-needed quality of life improvements, such as better customisation – the new top bar can be adjusted to display the tabs in order of preference, and the library can be filtered using a variety of categories.

In terms of what future updates will offer, Keely revealed that “the other piece that we're going to be working on is how to improve game discovery in a way that is relevant to each player. We have a pretty large library and sometimes there's great games that will be relevant for someone, so making sure that we continue to improve the merchandising components of how we make game discovery more possible and make that more social so that people can recommend games to each other and make that easy to share.”

Epic had previously detailed its plans for a new launcher earlier this year, where it said that its efforts would result in five times faster boot times . Of course, while speed is an issue, it may well take more than that to convince players – some remain convinced that the Epic Games Store will never be as good as Steam.

Matt Purslow is IGN's Executive Editor of Features.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto IV – The Legacy Review
articles.summary: Obsessively detailed and impressively timeless, GTA IV is the prototype for modern Grand Theft Auto.
articles.body:
I’m taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t come with any new IGN score, but they will re-examine what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release. By the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly rank in my long-term love for this series.

Today it’s time to revisit Liberty City in Grand Theft Auto IV.

Grand Theft Auto IV is smaller than GTA: San Andreas. Significantly so, if you exclude water, as its land area is reportedly around only one-quarter the size of San Andreas’s physical real estate. GTA IV also has markedly reduced vehicle variety, with much fewer of them overall and zero car customisation. It has no asset management, less mission variety, no RPG-inspired skill system, a pretty paltry list of cheats, and the only thing you can alter about lead character Niko Bellic is his outfit. In fact, if you weren’t around for the arrival of GTA IV, I think it’s fair enough that you may actually find yourself a little confused about its place in the series pantheon. That is, how could this apparently smaller game with overtly fewer features than its predecessor have instantly become not only the highest-rated GTA in the history of the series, but one of the highest rated games of all time, full stop? Well, the devil is in the details. Countless, unprecedented, incredible details.

For all his faults as an Eastern European war veteran with a shady past and a short temper, who may or may not have spent 106 minutes trying to kill Owen Wilson back in 2001, Niko Bellic has actually carved out a place as one of the most likeable and accessible characters in the franchise. Lured by his cousin Roman’s lies of wealth and opportunity, it’s easy to both sympathise with Niko’s disappointment at his first encounter with the American Dream, and share in his distaste for the various bastards of Liberty City who seek to exploit him.

Released in 2008, GTA IV was the first game in the series to be set in the present day since GTA III. In 2026, it’s an interesting snapshot of the world just prior to the smartphone takeover – back when the internet was still a destination you took time out to visit on a computer, social media was still a novelty rather than the worst thing to happen to humanity since disco music, and your radio would always let you know you were about to receive a mobile phone call. However, despite the 18 year gulf between its setting and today, GTA IV doesn’t feel remotely as retro as something like GTA: Vice City did in 2002 – even though there were only 16 years between its setting and the time of its release. The aesthetic distinctions between the ’80s and 2000s are, of course, profound. What are the visual differences between the 2000s and now, other than the fact The Rock used to have hair? It’s not a long list. Monoculture is dead, fashion is looping, and – as remarkably detailed as GTA IV is – I don’t think there’s anything Rockstar could have done to dodge this phenomenon, Dwayne Johnson’s shaven skull notwithstanding.

However, even though the feeling I glean from GTA IV being a depiction of a specific moment in time may not be as strong as that elicited by either GTA: Vice City or GTA: San Andreas, there is no denying what a victory it is in terms of its capacity to represent a true sense of place . GTA IV’s Liberty City wasn’t just one of the most convincing virtual cities of its generation; I honestly don’t think it’s an overstatement to say its commitment to tiny details still stands up to scrutiny today.

Revisiting GTA IV’s Liberty City in 2026 – a game that my Xbox 360 play data indicated to me I haven’t touched in around 14 years – I’m immediately reminded of how fastidiously crafted every corner of this world is. Yes, it’s a smaller environment than that of San Andreas, but it’s one that is so much more crowded, dense, and dripping with depth. It’s more immediate, more authentic, and more intimate than anything that came before it – and it’s still a more credible and convincing city than those in most of the open-world action games I’ve played since.

Strolling though Star Junction – Liberty City’s glitzy Times Square proxy – I find myself in tourist mode. I’m too engaged by the fact there’s something to see, read, or admire everywhere I point the camera to be distracted by the temptation of causing anti-social chaos. Hoofing it through Hove Beach – inspired by Brooklyn’s Brighton Beach – and I’m once again impressed at how much mileage Rockstar extracts from the seemingly mundane. Garbage strewn on the sidewalks. Individualised storefronts that are faithful to the demographics of the area and are never repeated elsewhere around the city. Places with stories you’ll never get to the bottom of. Like, who is Mikey Pissroll, and how much better at pool is he than Anal Alan?

The architecture, the lighting, the lived-in grime; Liberty City here feels more than real. It feels aged . Rockstar didn’t just build streets; it built them, and then assaulted that asphalt with decades of simulated wear. As a result, those streets are a patchwork of potholes, road plates, and sporadic strips of more recently re-surfaced segments. The custom signwork, the bespoke graffiti – the fact that no piece of the city looks like any other. A multitude of elements combine to create what was an unprecedented sense of immersion at the time, and absolutely still holds up today. Sure, there’s an unavoidable murkiness to playing GTA IV on original hardware like the Xbox 360, where you’re obviously beholden to the resolution limitations of its age. It results in a soft and rather muted image, and one that’s admittedly exacerbated by the overly cool and slightly washed out colour palette Rockstar opted for. However, it’s still a stunning place to simply explore, whether walking, driving, or using public transport – which is a viable and realistic way to move around this tightly-packed urban metropolis.

While Rockstar was committed to rebuilding its famous riff on New York City as realistically as possible within the fidelity it could muster at the time, it also placed an enormous emphasis on physical realism. The beating heart of this approach was NaturalMotion’s procedural character-animation technology, Euphoria – an animation and physics solution that completely transformed how people moved, reacted to impacts, and interacted with their surroundings. It wasn’t just a trivial technical flourish; it fundamentally altered the way the game felt to play, whether you were cutting enemies down with a barrage of bullets, or mercilessly bouncing them off the bonnet of an automobile. It reinvented GTA.

Traditional animation relies heavily on pre-authored movements, with developers creating and canning specific sequences that characters will perform in particular circumstances. That is, fill them with lead and they’ll sink to the ground the same way every time. Strike them with a car and they’ll fly up and flop down identically, regardless of the forces at work. Euphoria does away with all of this and, in 2008, it felt like a stunning glimpse of the future. Ditching those pre-determined animations, characters in GTA IV react realistically – both based on the forces impacting them, and the world within arm’s reach of them. A spray of gunfire may stagger an enemy into a railing behind, which they can tumble over dramatically. A well-placed shot may cause someone to lose their balance and fall off a ledge. Clipping someone in a car will skittle them in a totally different way to clobbering them head-on. One too many drinks may make putting one foot in front of the other temporarily tricky.

The results are often wildly slapstick – like when Niko flies through the windscreen after neglecting to use a seatbelt, or when NPCs insist on clutching the door handle of your car as it begins to peel away. I still live for these moments. In fact, I’ll often hesitate before getting on the throttle to allow carjacking victims a brief window to grab on before I take them on a brief trip to destination road rash. I don’t know what that says about me. Nothing good, probably.

So much of the endless experimentation on offer in GTA IV is a direct result of Euphoria, and the fact no two encounters will ever really play out the same way twice. But it also works because it’s part of a much wider commitment to granular realism. That is, what good is a world that oozes so much character and authenticity if the people feel painted on? Like they’re skating through it rather than actually inhabiting it? Everything about GTA IV is engineered to immerse us into its world; like we’re just another living, breathing citizen of Liberty City.

Despite the incredible critical acclaim GTA IV accumulated, it remains one of the more divisive games in the series. While I am quite partial to the slower nature of its more pragmatic story and straightforward missions as a change of pace, it wasn’t to everyone’s tastes, nor was the relationship system. It was a smart way to disseminate rewards for fostering relationships with your in-game friends, but it admittedly could’ve benefited from a larger range of activities to do with them around the city – and preferably ones that were a little more fun, too. As it stands, the relationship system is too chore-like, requiring you to repeat the same cycle: pick them up, head to one of a couple of venues, and drive them home.

Similarly, GTA IV’s extremely weighty driving physics are another controversial topic. For mine, I’ve actually always been quite partial to the feel of GTA IV, particularly in certain cars where I think the exaggerated body roll and sluggish steering makes sense – like muscle cars and beefy 4x4s. I would’ve liked some more sharpness in its range of sports cars and supercars – they should have stiffer suspension as they ought to be the cars with the firmest rides – but I do much prefer GTA IV’s approach to damage modeling over GTA V.

There also doesn’t seem to be any real consensus regarding the radio stations, either, with sentiment that swings between high praise for the outright station variety to claims the song list is the most forgettable in the series. I have to concede I lean towards the latter; coming off the immense highs of Vice City and San Andreas I remember being a little underwhelmed at the time – although the soundtrack expanded and improved quite noticeably following the arrival of The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony, the two smartest pieces of DLC Rockstar ever produced.

Sentimentally speaking, Grand Theft Auto IV isn’t my favourite of the series – but I would say it’s the one I respect the most. It was bold to dial things back from the unhinged freedom of San Andreas in favour of a slower paced and more grounded crime saga, but it was a decision that allowed Rockstar to establish the importance of having a city so detailed it became a character itself, as well as flex a tech solution for character animation that has gone on to be a defining pillar of the series’ brand of emergent, slapstick fun. Obsessively detailed and impressively timeless, GTA IV is the prototype for modern Grand Theft Auto.

For more reflections on the incredible Grand Theft Auto series, you can read our new Legacy Reviews of Grand Theft Auto , Grand Theft Auto 2 , Grand Theft Auto III , Grand Theft Auto: Vice City , and Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas .

Luke Reilly is an award-winning journalist with 23 years of media experience across Official PlayStation Magazine, Australian 360, and IGN – which he joined in 2011. You can find him on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering Designer's Response to Product Fatigue Sparks Debate About the Deluge of New Cards
articles.summary: There are a lot of Magic: The Gathering cards coming out these days, and there are a lot of Magic players who think there are too many. But fans don't need to pay attention to every MTG set — according to Magic game designer Mark Rosewater.
articles.body:
There are a lot of Magic: The Gathering cards coming out these days, and there are a lot of Magic players who think there are too many . But fans don't need to pay attention to every set — according to Magic game designer Mark Rosewater.

Last night, Rosewater posted to his Tumblr to answer a question from a fan about the product fatique players feel from having six Magic sets every year. He replied: "We did some research on this. It turns out a very small minority of Magic players feels a need to track every newly released card. Obviously, this audience tends to be very enfranchised, so they’re over represented online."

"The game already has over 33,000 unique cards," he added. "We’re well past the mark where any one player can mentally track everything."

Magic: The Gathering – Marvel Darkhold Destiny New Cards

And it doesn't seem like Wizards of the Coast plans to slow things down any time soon, even if some enfranchised players — myself included — are sometimes fatigued by the sheer amount of cards that come out every year.

In the same blog post, Rosewater added: "Limiting how many cards we release per year to how many cards this small group can comfortably mentally track just doesn’t make good business sense. Our upper limit needs to be guided by what players are purchasing and playing, not by how easy it is to track everything new." So, essentially the deluge of new Magic cards will continue as long as sales support them.

Of course, there were a lot of these 'enfranchised' Magic players who didn't love Rosewater's answer here. Over on Reddit, the post was shared to the tune of over 1,300 upvotes, and while there are definitely some who agree with Rosewater's approach, there were a lot of people who were upset by it. User GunTotingQuaker replied : "I embraced the 'every product isn’t for everyone' thing years ago. There are going to be 5,000 new cards a year, deal with it or don’t. My issue is it feels like every time I dust off a 1+ year old EDH deck to see what I might update… it’s like half the f***ing deck."

MTG player Amarsir was also upset , but this time by how the volume of cards affects the Standard format. "Does he not remember Standard?" they asked. "I mean I can understand forgetting it exists. But the whole concept is knowing each new set. Commander players don't need to know every card. But they didn't go from 8-set Standard to 18-set to affect Commander players now did they?"

However, there were plenty of folks who did agree with Rosewater, with some, like user MoO, simply saying : "Folks should take the same attitude towards Magic releases as the news: unplug for a bit when it’s too much, it’s healthier."

Others questioned how many cards anyone has to realistically pay attention to at any one time, like TunefulTunic , who asked "can standard players tell me, do you really need to know every single card that comes out in a set like a lot of people here claim?", to which Kanin_usagi replied "The lands are important to know I suppose, and then familiar with planeswalkers and the major archetypes. Otherwise most sets really only have like 25-ish cards that will see any major play. Right now I’m not even sure Final Fantasy or Ixalan have any non-lands that see play."

Either way, it doesn't seem like Magic sets are slowing down any time soon. There were seven total sets in 2026, with Reality Fracture being the most recent, and with the Star Trek crossover launching next month. 2027 will be a bit slower, with only six sets, but they should all be full sets, where both Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and The Hobbit this year were smaller sets with fewer cards.

Wizards of the Coast recently announced its first Universes Beyond set for 2027 at New York Comic Con , but unlike 2025's Spider-Man or 2026's Marvel Superheroes, Darkhold Destiny will see the Magic team creating its own Magic-flavored story with Marvel characters.

articles.title: Whalefall Review: Austin Abrams Carries This Terrifying and Immensely Claustrophobic Movie About a Guy Trying to Escape the Belly of a Whale
articles.summary: Whalefall, directed by Brian Duffield based on Daniel Kraus' novel of the same name, pulls the viewer into an unthinkably frightening, incredibly gross, and panic-inducing environment that plays on primal human fears about being predator or prey. As visceral as the film is, Whalefall is ultimately a moving story about grief and the gulf that can develop between fathers and sons. An exceptional Austin Abrams anchors the whole endeavor with grueling dedication.
articles.body:
The new survival thriller Whalefall checked a number of my phobia boxes going into it, so my critical response to the film was always going to be measured by how much it triggered these primal fears of mine. And (I guess?) I’m happy to report the film did that too damn well at times.

Assuredly directed by Brian Duffield and based on Daniel Kraus’ bestselling book of the same name , Whalefall has a simple yet incredibly compelling premise: Young scuba diver Jay Gardiner ( Resident Evil’s Austin Abrams ) is swallowed by a massive sperm whale and must figure out how to escape from the belly of the beast while his oxygen supply lasts. He has an hour of air left so his struggle basically plays out in real time on screen.

What happens inside the whale’s belly is brought to life with gruesome, excruciating and claustrophobic intensity by Duffield and his team of artists. (They built a whale’s belly, for Jonah’s sake!) There are so many awful ways for Jay to die in there before his oxygen runs out, whether it’s being crushed by the whale’s innards, or succumbing to all the gnarly injuries he sustains from the toxic environment or the other sea creatures the whale has swallowed that are also still alive.

Deeper emotional layers are added to the story by revealing why Jay was diving that day to begin with: He was searching for the remains of his dad, Mitt (Josh Brolin), a well-liked diver and whale-watching boat skipper in their Central California community. Suffering from mesothelioma, which robbed him of being able to dive and connect with nature, Mitt drowned himself in the opening scene rather than continue suffering.

Jay refused to see his father in his final days after a volatile falling out. Jay’s grief and guilt over his strained relationship with his gruff, tough love dad has consumed him and, as he desperately tries to find a way to escape the whale, flashbacks to the lessons Mitt drilled into him about diving and nature prove vital to his slim chances of trying to MacGyver his way out of this ordeal.

Whalefall is a visceral, grueling survival tale, but what distinguishes it in the man vs. nature/beast genre is that it’s really about a father and son who don’t know how to communicate with each other. It’s not until he’s near death himself that Jay starts to truly understand his father and find peace. This makes the third act pretty trippy as the symbolism of the whale and its role in nature is intertwined with Jay’s oxygen-deprived thoughts about Mitt. This device inches right up to the edge of absurdity but thankfully never plummets into it. It’s weird but sincere and moving enough to work.

As Mitt, Brolin is basically Robert Duvall in The Great Santini crossed with Quint from Jaws. He looks like a Hell’s Angel, talks like a New Age hippie, and is basically able to get along with everyone but his son. In the hands of a less skilled actor, the character could have been unbearable but Brolin makes him flesh and blood and, ultimately, vulnerable.

But this is Austin Abrams’ movie, full stop, and he carries it with amazing commitment.

As Jay, Abrams is put through the wringer physically, with the camera in his face the whole hour he’s trapped inside the whale, so there’s never a moment he can't deliver an authentic reaction to what’s unfolding. He conveys so much emotion with just his eyes and some grunts (he wears a scuba mouthpiece for nearly the entire time inside the whale so he can’t speak clearly). In the scenes on land, Abrams keeps the college-aged Jay from seeming like a petulant brat, his emotional avoidance more a survival mechanism than something less mature.

articles.title: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 is a Gore-geous, Pixelated Boomer Shooter That Builds on the Original
articles.summary: With two main characters in a replayable old-school FPS campaign, Boltgun 2 elevates the bloody action of the Warhammer universe.
articles.body:
Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 wastes no time hooking you into its blistering, blood-soaked world. Seriously, there are only a few minutes of speedy exposition before you're sent diving through a battered spaceship, hurling bullets and slicing rogue enemy agents to pieces – all while shouting sanctimonious battle cries as innards slosh against the tarnished metal flooring. With a breakneck pace and plenty of pixelated gore, it's clear developer Auroch Digital isn't messing with the magic in this first-person shooter sequel. Instead, the team has elevated the original's frantic run-and-gun style with boosted enemy counts and demanding level objectives that'll have you shouting 'For the Emperor.'

Boltgun 2's story kicks off with a literal bang; your ship is destroyed at the hands of the Great Daemon Vashtorr. Hungry for revenge, you respond (somewhat reasonably by Warhammer standards, might I add) by launching a brutal intergalactic campaign, fighting through bile-filled swamps to demonic dwellings, frozen facilities, and beyond. Joined by a sassy Servo-skull companion to guide you through the crimson haze, your mission is all about survival, clearing out hordes of vicious heretics while collecting enough ammunition and health kits at a cadence that's unapologetically old-school. It's repetitive by its very nature, and the story can feel a bit like Warhammer word salad at times. Still, thanks to the mesmerising enemy designs and level variety, as well as the breakneck pace, it's easy to enter a flow state of slicing and dicing through some of Games Workshop's most imposing baddies.

There are four difficulty options to work through, ranging from Low, where your health is bolstered and your damage increased, to Exterminatus, which is about as terrifying as the term would imply. For those looking for more control, you'll also have your pick of game-modifying settings like the ability to disable head bobbing and screen shake, or toggle on invulnerability, too. While I opted to play on the recommended Medium difficulty – with the campaign taking around eight or so hours per protagonist – it's nice to see Boltgun 2 accounts for all kinds of player preferences here.

While there's a lot to shout about, my favourite new feature in Boltgun 2 is the addition of a second playable character. Joining the first Boltgun's Space Marine Malum Caedo is the badass Sister of Battle, Nyra Veyrath. While both are fanatical in their devotion, as often heard in their intense, toggleable taunts, the major difference between them lies in their combat styles. Where Caedo is akin to a hulking mech kitted out with a buzzing Chainsword and frag grenades, Veyrath is much more nimble, wielding a Powersword and hefty Melta Bomb. They feel pleasantly distinct in both their personalities and weaponry. Initially, I was enamoured with Veyrath's Fervent Slide attack, which lets you blitz forward and bisect any fodder in your way, but in playing Caedo's campaign, I was equally enamored by his Chainsword Lunge, which felt more decisive and controlled, great for dealing with squishy hordes. All this to say, there really is no wrong option when choosing your warrior, and the thrill of playing as either adds to the replayability of Boltgun 2, further emphasized by the campaign's branching level options.

As you complete levels, you'll make cartographical choices throughout Boltgun 2's campaign to determine your path forward. Alongside a few optional side missions, there are specific battle locations you'll have to choose between as you advance to the big finale. On my first playthrough as Veyrath, I had to choose between dropping into a dense rainforest overrun with blight or working through a fortified beachhead with enemies hidden in sandy trenches. While I initially opted for the former, it was energizing to know that on a second playthrough, not only could I choose an alternative character with a unique loadout, but I would also have entirely new levels waiting for me.

This dynamism extends into Boltgun 2's mission objectives, too, which often have you descending into a scourge-filled hellhole to manage a few rounds of gladiatorial combat and heroically escape. It sounds familiar on paper, but each level has tricks up its sleeve. In one location, I was blowing up blood tanks to weaken a Daemonic construct, and in another, I was working my way down a vertical chamber, breaking through panes of ice to drop enemies into the blades of a whirring fan. The surprising diversity of what you're tasked with does a good job of keeping progression fresh, mitigating the dreaded shooter fatigue from setting in.

That's not all, though, as each map has location-specific quirks to consider. Alongside Purges, which occur periodically and lock you into areas until you've painted the floor red, certain combat conditions introduce more complexity. This time around, you aren't always alone in battle, and are occasionally joined by friendly soldiers who help keep morale high and serve as convenient meat shields when the moment arrives. Additionally, there are plenty of physical hazards, from flaming pools to thick fog that clouds your vision. These moving parts not only amp up the chaos but also create ingenious cover for Boltgun 2's well-hidden collectibles: the combat-buffing Secrets and collectible Seals.

Though for all its guts and glory, Boltgun 2 unfortunately suffers from a handful of technical issues. Enemies can occasionally forget they're in a holy war and wander around idly like NPCs. While hardly a threat to survival, it does take you out of the action to see a roughed-up creep dawdling. Elsewhere, the infamous Purges sometimes wouldn't end, and despite killing every heretic, I found myself stuck waiting for an exit to unlock… but it never did. The movement isn't completely airtight either. It's suitable for dancing around a combat arena or jumping between and scaling platforms, but it can feel slippery when tackling the more ambitious platforming challenges that arrive in the latter half of the campaign. Though it's a list of annoyances that can give cause for concern, these issues are by no means dealbreakers when set against the slick shooting and spectacle that's so distinctly Warhammer.

I have to hand it to the art team at Auroch Digital because beyond the frenetic combat, Boltgun 2's strongest asset is by far its retro aesthetic. I've spent hundreds of hours toiling over miniatures and painting intricate details to make them pop, so perhaps I have a soft spot for these characters, but Boltgun 2 captures that digitised figure look with sharp precision. The way they appear and move fits the nostalgic boomer shooter dressing perfectly. And, while it's hard to pick favourites, I can't deny that the visually assaulting Daemonettes and the towering, beast-riding Bloodcrushers were particular standouts, their violent animations and vivid palettes both delightful and terrifying. If you pay attention, there's personality embedded in almost every character model, too. As you approach them in battle, you might notice a Tormentor flicking a knife around or a tiny Nurgling mooning you mid-attack. These kinds of fine details aren't necessarily essential and could easily be overlooked, but their incorporation speaks to an attention to detail at the core of Boltgun 2 that makes it such a compelling extension of the Warhammer universe.

The atmosphere is further heightened by adrenaline-bolstering, context-specific barks that your chosen protagonist can let off at the tap of a button. Rahul Kohli delivers an impressively commanding performance in his reprisal of Caedo, and Alanah Pearce's Veyrath is fittingly vicious. Similarly, I enjoyed the writing behind the aforementioned Servo-skull, my eternally irreverent companion who would lighten tricky combat situations with lines like, "Blood Ingress detected in the ocular module." It's one thing to engage me with combat; it's another to get a genuine laugh out of me – and Boltgun 2 manages to do both.

articles.title: Tezuka! God of Manga Documentary Celebrates the Iconic Astro Boy Creator
articles.summary: With the documentary film Tezuka! God of Manga now on Kickstarter, IGN can exclusively reveal some of the gorgeous art prints included in the campaign.
articles.body:
There's no doubt that Osamu Tezuka belongs on the Mt. Rushmore of legendary manga creators. His work on Astro Boy alone cements his status as one of the most important figures in the medium. That creative legacy is being explored in a new documentary called Tezuka! God of Manga.

With the Kickstarter campaign for Tezuka! God of Manga live now, IGN can exclusively debut a new set of art prints being included in the campaign. Check them out in the slideshow gallery below:

Tezuka! God of Manga is directed by Jason Andrew Cohn. Here's the official description of the film:

TEZUKA! God of Manga will feature interviews with legendary manga and anime creators including Katsuhiro Otomo (Akira), Riyoko Ikeda (Rose of Versaille), Naoki Urasawa (Monster), Go Nagai (Devilman), Yoshiyuki Tomino (Gundam), MADHOUSE co-founder and anime producer Masao Maruyama (Tokyo Godfathers), anime director Rintaro (Metropolis), best-selling fantasy author Ada Palmer (Too Like the Lightning), Samuel Sattin (Unico Awakening), and Jorge R. Gutierrez (The Book of Life), to discuss how Tezuka’s trailblazing influenced their work and changed the mediums of manga, comics, and animation.

The documentary will also include in-depth conversations with scholars Helen McCarthy (The Art of Osamu Tezuka), Natsu Onoda Power (God of Comics: Osamu Tezuka and the creation of post-World War II Manga), and the dean of English-language manga scholarship, Fred Schodt (Manga! Manga!) discussing his long working relationship with Tezuka. Once the film is funded, the producers will schedule additional interviews with artists including Paul Pope (THB) and Ron Wimberly (Prince of Cats).

“TEZUKA! God of Manga celebrates Tezuka-sensei as a preposterously prolific, enigmatic creator who forever altered popular culture by introducing young readers to a brand-new, DIY medium that rocketed around the world,” said Cohn in a statement. “The creative cross-fertilization between artists in Japan and the rest of the world made Tezuka one of the most beloved and influential artists of the 20th century. This film will celebrate his legacy and introduce his incredible creations to a new generation.”

articles.title: Anbernic’s next dual-screen handheld could replace your aging Nintendo 3DS
articles.summary: Anbernic’s RG DDS closely replicates the Nintendo 3DS but skips the 3D screen for other modern upgrades including higher resolution displays.
articles.body: Anbernic shared a new video of its upcoming dual-screen handheld it announced last week showing the device playing 3DS, Xbox, and PS3 games through emulation. While competitors like Ayaneo have been making dual-screen handhelds for a few years, Anbernic only recently introduced its own dual-screen devices including the RG DS and RG DS Plus. Those handhelds are designed to be modern replacements for the Nintendo DS, but the new RG DDS, short for “Dream Dual Screen,” has a faster processor and displays with aspect ratios optimized to replace the Nintendo 3DS — although Anbernic isn’t trying to recreate the glasses-free 3D effect. Full performance details aren’t yet known, and Anbernic has yet to reveal the RG DDS’ price or how aggressively it plans to compete with devices like the Ayaneo Pocket DS which currently starts at $579. Both the Anbernic RG DS and DS Plus start at under $100. [Image: The RG DDS will initially be available in three color options: blue, white, and black. What we do know is that the RG DDS will feature a 4.7-inch, 1,200x720 top screen and a 4-inch, 960x720 bottom display that match the aspect ratios of what the 3DS used. Those displays also both feature triple the resolution of the 3DS’ screens allowing emulated games to be easily scaled up. The RG DDS will be powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon G2 Gen 2 chipset with a 6,000mAh rechargeable battery and will include built-in vibration feedback and an extendable stylus stashed inside. [Image: Anbernic says it has developed a new control center for the handheld that’s accessible on the RG DDS’ lower touchscreen. The RG DDS’ design looks nearly identical to the 3DS although you’ll find an additional analog thumbstick on the lower right for playing 3D games that require a pair of them. It also carries forward the small button found next to the top right corner of Nintendo’s New 3DS’ touchscreen. articles.summary: Get an exclusive look at Johnny Depp's extensive makeup transformation into Ebenezer Scrooge for the upcoming film Ebenezer, plus a reveal of the brand-new movie poster.
articles.body:
Johnny Depp’s take on the classic Christmas Carol story arrives next month, but we have an exclusive look at his transformation into the iconic Ebenezer Scrooge just in time for IGN Fan Fest.

Depp stars in the upcoming film Ebenezer and, as you can see in the exclusive video below, he underwent extensive makeup and prosthetic work for the role.

“I’ll be honest, the first time I saw him in full makeup I did not recognize him,” says Depp’s co-star Trammell Tillman, who plays the Ghost of Christmas Present. “Johnny was really excited to play Scrooge in his own way.

“Johnny really embraces the makeup process,” says Barrie Gower, Prosthetic Designer on the film. “He’s suggesting things like moles. He wanted his chin a little longer, anything that we can add to the character.”

In addition to a brand-new look at the movie, we can exclusively reveal a new poster for Ebenezer, which you can see below. The image showcases an up-close look at Depp’s Scrooge, along with Tillman’s Ghost of Christmas Present, the Ghost of Christmas Future (Robert Strange), and the Ghost of Christmas Past (Andrea Riseborough).

Depp’s co-stars on the film say the actor, known for transforming himself for roles like Pirates of the Caribbean’s Captain Jack Sparrow and Alice in Wonderland’s Mad Hatter, relished the opportunity to tackle character.

“I think he brings something unique to everything he does,” says Rupert Grint, who plays Bob Cratchit in the film. “I think this is such a perfect role for him.”

“Johnny is giving a performance the likes of which you’ve never seen before,” says Ian McKellen, who plays Marley. “But that’s what you expect with Johnny Depp, isn’t it? He’s full of surprises.”

“It’s Johnny doing what Johnny does best,” says Daisy Ridley, who plays Clara. “Which are these larger-than-life characters with a real human touch.”

Ebenezer arrives in theaters November 13.

articles.body:
Apple recently announced a selection of new devices for your home that will be available in the coming weeks. These include the new Apple TV 4K with an A19 chip, the HomePod mini 2 , and the brand-new Apple HomeView , which acts as a hub for your smart home devices. All the new Apple devices are up for preorder at Amazon and/or elsewhere. Let’s take a look.

Above, you'll find a cheat sheet of sorts for where to preorder these upcoming items. You'll find all of the retailer links below, along with details about each new item.

Apple’s one brand-new product in the recent announcement is Apple HomeView. It’s a Siri AI-equipped device with a screen and a speaker that you put in the kitchen or other central area in your household. It can have up to six users and can do a lot of different things, including manage your lights, doorbell, cameras, and other smart home devices (the full list of compatible items is here ).

It can also access each user’s data to answer questions or pull up recipes or directions from your messages or maps app. It can do FaceTime calls and play music and all sorts of other things, too.

Apple HomeView is available to preorder now in four subtle color options for $299. You can get it with a stand to set on your counter, or without to be mounted on a wall. However, Amazon is already offering a discount, bringing select models down to $289.99.

The latest version of the Apple TV 4K runs on an A19 chip, which Apple says makes it up to 50% faster compared to the previous model. That means it’ll load your streaming apps faster and run Apple Arcade games better.

It also has Siri AI capabilities baked in (as long as you’ve paired the device with a recent iPad or iPhone). The new Apple TV has long-range microphones that let you talk to the digital assistant without having to press any buttons, which is pretty convenient. It costs $299 and is out November 13.

The HomePod mini 2 represents the first new hardware improvements on Apple’s smart speaker in six years. It looks similar to the previous model, but it packs the S10 chip, making it faster and more responsive. It also features Sound Glow lighting, Siri AI support (coming in a later update), and home theater capabilities. It’s not available for preorder on Amazon (yet?), but it’s available at all the other retailers.

Preorders for Apple's new folding phone aren't live yet (they start at 5 a.m. PT on Friday, October 16), but you can prepare your preorder now at Apple . You can sign in and make your selections, like color and storage size, as well as set up your trade-in, if applicable. Then, once preorders do go live, you'll be able to check out quickly.

articles.title: Microsoft Announces Xbox Nano Controller, a Tiny New Gamepad That Fits in Your Pocket
articles.summary: Xbox controllers are already the default option for a whole range of devices, from the Xbox itself to gaming PCs and tablets. But Microsoft has just announced the Nano Controller, a smaller and cheaper Xbox controller.
articles.body:
Xbox controllers are already the default option for a whole range of devices, from the Xbox itself to gaming PCs and tablets. But Microsoft has just announced the Nano Controller, a smaller and cheaper Xbox controller.

The Xbox Nano controller is essentially just a smaller Xbox Series X controller , and while Microsoft's blog doesn't share exact measurements, it is "about 5 inches" long and weighs 3.5 ounces, which is much smaller and lighter than the existing Xbox controller. The Nano Controller is also more affordable, coming in at $49.99, rather than the $69.99 that Microsoft typically charges for a controller. It's available to preorder now.

But while the Nano controller will be compatible with Xbox consoles, the focus here is on other devices like smart TVs, laptops, and any other device that, until recently, Microsoft would have claimed to be an Xbox. To that end, Microsoft is teaming up with Samsung to bundle the new Xbox Nano controller, along with two months of Game Pass with "select Samsung TVs" over the holiday season.

According to Microsoft's blog , the company is also working on a deal with Meta to include the Nano Controller, along with a Game Pass subscription to new Meta Quest owners, but it doesn't sound like that deal is quite set in stone. Still, Microsoft is targeting a holiday release for that, too.

Of course, the compatibility will stretch even further than just Samsung TVs and Meta Quest. Becuase the controller has both the standard Xbox wireless connection, along with Bluetooth, the Nano Controller should work with pretty much any device that supports Bluetooth. So, you could use this to play Fortnite on your iPad, if you're so inclined.

But while the Xbox Nano controller is Microsoft's first foray into mini controllers, it's far from an original concept. Companies like CRKD and 8BitDo have been selling mini controllers for years, and the selling point is the portability. With a controller this small, it's incredibly easy to slip it into a bag and take it wherever you go, without taking up too much space or adding a lot of heft to your bag.

This isn't the only thing that Microsoft's controller team has been working on. For months, there have been leaks suggesting that the new Xbox Elite Series 3 controller is right around the corner , and might even fix some of its predecessor's compatibility problems.

The Xbox Nano Controller will be available starting in November, and you can preorder it now. But as for the partnerships with Samsung and Meta, we'll likely just have to wait until those companies announce more details as the holiday season approaches.
